planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in fall or early spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Simplex is a named selection of the single-flowered wild form and closely resembles the unimproved species.

directions: Simplex is an RHS-listed selection of the wild single-flowered form of Japanese kerria, chosen and named to preserve the unimproved type rather than to introduce a new trait. It produces solitary, five-petaled, bright yellow flowers along prominently veined light green leaves in mid-spring, on arching, bright green canes that hold their color through winter. The shrub suckers vigorously from the base and can spread into a substantial colony if left unchecked, so remove a portion of old canes and stray suckers at ground level each winter to keep it in bounds. It tolerates deep shade better than most flowering shrubs, making it useful for difficult woodland-edge or foundation sites where little else blooms.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Shannon is a larger, more vigorous single-flowered selection than the straight species and benefits from afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Shannon is a vigorous, extra-large-flowered single selection of Japanese kerria, regarded by growers as one of the finest single-flowered forms available. Clear golden-yellow, five-petaled flowers up to two and a half inches across open profusely from March into May on arching, deep green canes, with scattered rebloom through summer in cooler climates. It grows larger and more robust than the straight species, reaching four to five feet, and performs best in dappled shade under high tree canopy or on the shaded side of a building. In hot, humid regions, shield it from harsh afternoon sun to prevent foliage scorch.

common_name: Fubuki Nishiki Kerria (Patented White-Flecked Variegated Japanese Rose)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; give Fubuki Nishiki room to spread since its habit becomes wide and pendulous with age.

directions: Fubuki Nishiki is a patented Japanese-origin sport distinguished by irregular white flecking, splashing, and mottling covering roughly a quarter to half of each leaf, on foliage slightly larger than the plain-green species. Flowers are soft yellow overlaid with lighter yellow and greyed-green variegation rather than the solid gold of the parent plant, opening amid the patterned foliage in spring. Young plants grow upright and multi-branched, but by the second and third year the habit becomes increasingly wide-spreading and gracefully pendulous, eventually reaching roughly six feet tall and nearly ten feet across. Because reversion to plain green growth can occur on older wood, prune out any solid-green shoots promptly to preserve the variegation.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office (Plant Patent USPP15,247)
Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Shandale Kerria (Cat's Eye Variegated Japanese Rose)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade; Shandale keeps a more compact, upright habit than most kerria and works well in containers.

directions: Shandale, marketed under the trademark Cat's Eye, is a patented variegated sport discovered on the large-flowered cultivar 'Shannon'. Its green leaves are irregularly margined and splashed with creamy white, brightening shaded corners through the growing season, while slender green canes add further winter interest after leaf drop. Dark golden-yellow single flowers open in mid to late spring against the variegated foliage, giving stronger color contrast than many other variegated kerria selections. It keeps a more compact, upright, freely branching habit than its parent, making it well suited to containers or small shade gardens where a spreading shrub would be too large.
sources: United States Patent and Trademark Office (Plant Patent PP21,975)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free gardens (zones 9-10) or start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost in colder climates; refracta is one of the original wild species behind modern hybrid freesias and does best in gritty, fast-draining soil.

directions: Freesia refracta is one of the original South African species brought into cultivation in the late eighteenth century and used to breed many of today's hybrid freesias, though it remains distinct and still grown in its own right. Its slender stems carry pale greenish-yellow to dull white flowers, often flushed purplish outside, with bright orange nectar guides on the lower petals, and a fragrance that ranges from unscented to a strong rose-and-violet perfume depending on the population. In its native dry, stony slopes of the southwestern Cape it blooms in the local winter-to-spring season; in Northern Hemisphere gardens this translates to a late-winter to spring bloom from fall-planted corms. Grow it in the same lean, sharply drained conditions used for other winter-growing South African corms, and let foliage die back naturally before withholding water for summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free gardens (zones 9-10) or start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost in colder climates; viridis wants the same lean, dry-summer regimen as other winter-growing Cape corms.

directions: Freesia viridis is a novelty species grown for its unusual green flowers, heavily flushed brown or maroon rather than the yellow, white, or pink tones typical of most freesias. Some wild populations are unscented during the day but release a distinct rose fragrance after dark, an adaptation that likely reflects pollination by night-flying insects. It is native to the winter-rainfall coastal strip from Namibia south to just north of Cape Town, where it grows low to the ground on sandy flats. In cultivation it wants the same lean, gritty, fast-draining soil, full sun, and dry summer dormancy as other winter-growing Cape corms, and suits a collector's bulb frame or alpine trough more than a general flower bed.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free gardens (zones 9-10) or start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost in colder climates; choose divisions or seed strains of known provenance since wild populations vary considerably in size.

directions: Freesia occidentalis bears creamy white to pale creamy-yellow flowers, sometimes flushed mauve or pink, marked with bright yellow nectar guides, and carries an unusual rosy-violet fragrance with a peppery edge that sets it apart from sweeter freesia scents. It flowers later in the season than many Cape freesias, opening from midsummer into early autumn in its native arid fynbos and low shrubland of the northwestern Cape and western Karoo. Height is quite variable between populations, from under four inches to about twenty inches, so named divisions of known provenance give more predictable results in the garden. Provide the same lean, sharply drained, summer-dry conditions as other winter-growing South African corms, in full sun with excellent air movement.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in frost-free gardens (zones 9-10) or start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost in colder climates; its near-prostrate size suits a shallow pan or the front edge of a raised bed.

directions: Freesia caryophyllacea is the most diminutive species in the genus, forming a near-prostrate dwarf plant only a few inches tall and best suited to a shallow pan or the front edge of a raised bed. Its Latin name means clove-scented, describing the sweet, spicy perfume of the white flowers, which are flushed purple on the reverse and marked with yellow-orange nectar guides. In its native Western Cape habitat it grows on gravelly clay, sandy coastal soil, and limestone ridges, and its diminutive size means it is easily overwhelmed by taller companions. Grow it away from crowding neighbors in the same fast-draining, dry-summer regimen used for other Cape winter-growing corms.
